title: India Embeds Ayurveda and Yoga in Global Trade Deals as Experts Press for Standards
excerpt: Three major trade agreements with the EU, Oman, and New Zealand include formal provisions for AYUSH systems, but credible evidence and regulation remain the missing pieces.
body:
• Three major trade agreements since early 2026 — with the EU, Oman, and New Zealand — include formal provisions for Ayurveda, Yoga, and other AYUSH systems.
  • The India-New Zealand FTA features a dedicated annex with practitioner mobility pathways and visa quotas for AYUSH professionals.
  • Experts warn that credible standards, evidence, and patient safety frameworks must keep pace with the diplomatic push.
  • Data gaps make it difficult to assess AYUSH's actual share of India's growing medical tourism market.

Trade Pacts Carve Formal Pathways

India has moved to formalize its traditional medicine systems as recognized health services in international trade, embedding Ayurveda, Yoga, and other AYUSH disciplines into three major trade agreements operationalized since the start of 2026, according to The Hindu.

The India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, operational since June 2026, includes what the government describes as its first comprehensive commitment on traditional medicine across all modes of supply. The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement goes further with a dedicated annex covering Ayurveda, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa, and Homoeopathy, complete with structured mobility pathways and a dedicated visa quota for AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors.

The India-European Union FTA, signed in January 2026, allows AYUSH practitioners to use their Indian qualifications in EU countries where no existing regulatory framework exists and provides for the establishment of AYUSH wellness centres and clinics.

From Cultural Export to Health Diplomacy

The trade provisions represent a significant shift in how India positions its traditional medicine systems globally — moving from cultural soft power to formalized health services backed by treaty commitments. The push builds on years of institutional groundwork, including the establishment of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre in Jamnagar, Gujarat, in 2022, the first facility of its kind, focused on data analytics, policy support, standard-setting, and research collaboration.

In May 2025, India supported the adoption of the new WHO Global Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034 at the World Health Assembly in Geneva. A key milestone followed when the Ministry of Ayush signed a donor agreement with the WHO to develop a dedicated Traditional Medicine module under the International Classification of Health Interventions, which would enable AYUSH systems to reach a global audience through a standardized framework, according to the Press Information Bureau.

Between January 2023 and December 2025, 3,375 foreign nationals traveled to India on Ayush visas, while another 579 came on Ayush attendant visas, according to ministry data. Under the Ayush Fellowship Scheme, 260 students from 32 countries are currently studying AYUSH disciplines in Indian institutions.

The Standards Question

The diplomatic push has sharpened a longstanding concern: whether India's AYUSH systems can meet the evidence and safety standards demanded by increasingly regulated global healthcare markets. Experts emphasize the need for credible standards, robust evidence, effective regulation, practitioner quality, and patient safety as prerequisites for AYUSH to gain traction abroad, according to The Hindu.

The India-New Zealand agreement attempts to address these concerns by institutionalizing cooperation in education, training, standards development, and wellness services. But the gap between diplomatic commitments and ground-level implementation remains wide.

Data Gaps Cloud the Picture

Assessing the actual impact of India's AYUSH diplomacy is complicated by significant data gaps. While foreign medical arrivals rose from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.44 lakh in 2024, that figure covers all foreign medical arrivals — not specifically AYUSH patients. The government does not publish consolidated country-wise rankings of AYUSH patients, making it difficult to measure AYUSH's actual share of India's medical-value-travel market.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For millions of Indian-origin residents in the EU, New Zealand, and the Gulf states, the trade provisions could eventually mean better access to qualified Ayurveda and Yoga practitioners operating within recognized legal frameworks. The India-EU FTA's recognition of Indian AYUSH qualifications is particularly relevant for diaspora communities in countries like Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK, where demand for Ayurvedic treatments has grown steadily.

What's Next

The trade agreements are operational, but much depends on implementation. Whether the visa quotas, practitioner recognition pathways, and wellness centre provisions translate into meaningful adoption will hinge on India's ability to demonstrate credible evidence for AYUSH treatments and build the regulatory infrastructure that global healthcare markets demand.
